title: Three-scenario latency & cost casebook
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact casebook contrasting latency and unit-cost outcomes across three representative production scenarios. The goal is to help PMs and platform leads pick practical knobs (batching, cache, quantization, routing) for target SLA bands and expected load profiles.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- We evaluated three realistic workloads: 1) conversational assistant with microbursts, 2) high-throughput embeddings pipeline, 3) mixed multimodal assistant (images + text).
- Hardware profiled: A100-80 (dedicated), T4 (economy), and an NVLink-pooled A100 equivalent (burst pool).
- Main trade-off: aggressive batching + 4-bit quantization cuts token cost ~2.2-3.1x but increases p99 latency by 1.6x–3.8x depending on burstiness. KV prefix caching reduces cost for conversation-style stateful workloads by ~15–40% with negligible p50 impact.
- Practical recommendation: For interactive assistants with p99 <= 600ms target, prefer modest batching (batch windows <=10ms) + selective KV cache; for embeddings choose larger micro-batches and use quantized-only variants.

Methodology (short):
- Scenarios driven from customer telemetry buckets and PM-provided templates.
- Synthetic driver with real token-length distributions: (assistant sessions: mean turn 120 tokens, heavy-tails to 2k; embeddings: 512 tokens; multimodal: 50 tokens + 1 image decode ~20ms).
- Simulated arrival processes: Poisson baseline + Weibull bursts for microburst stress.
- Config knobs sampled: batch window (0ms, 10ms, 50ms), KV cache (on/off, prefix sizes), quantization (fp16, int8, q4), route policy (dedicated first, burst-pool fallback).
- Cost model: GPU-minutes * cost-per-GPU + amortized infra (network, storage) scaled to per-1M-token baseline. We used Redwood internal cost rates (A100-80: $3.80/hr equivalent, T4: $0.60/hr equivalent, burst premium applied where noted).

Scenario A: Interactive assistant (microburst-heavy)
Context: Proactive chat assistant where users type short messages and expect low-latency replies. SLO targets: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 280ms, p99 < 600ms. High arrival variance: 80% of sessions produce 1–3 turns, 10% produce long sessions.
Key observations:
- No batching (0ms window) on A100 gives p50=95ms, p95=220ms, p99=480ms; cost baseline = $12.8 per 1M tokens.
- 10ms batching: p50=110ms, p95=240ms, p99=620ms; cost = $9.6 per 1M tokens (-25%).
- 50ms batching: p50=160ms, p95=380ms, p99=980ms; cost = $6.5 per 1M tokens (-49%) but violates p99 target.
- KV prefix cache (hot 25% of prefixes): reduces token emulation work and cuts cost by ~18% at 0ms batching; at 10ms batching it stacks to ~35% total savings because cached prefixes avoid longer generation steps.

ASCII chart (Scenario A, p99 vs batch window):
batch-window | p99-ms | cost-per-1M-tokens
0ms          | 480    | $12.8
10ms         | 620    | $9.6
50ms         | 980    | $6.5

Interpretation: There is a steep p99 cliff after ~20ms windows in microburst conditions. Small batching wins cost without catastrophic latency penalties; large windows break interactive SLOs.

Scenario B: High-throughput embeddings pipeline
Context: Bulk processing of documents into embeddings for search index updates. Throughput target: sustained 5k reqs/min with large batches acceptable; latency per request is soft (median acceptable up to 3s).
Key observations:
- Aggregating to 256-item micro-batches on T4 with int8 quantized model yields p50=1.2s, p95=2.9s; cost = $1.9 per 1M tokens equivalent (embeddings measured per 1k items here).
- Moving to A100 with large batches (1024) reduces p50 to 0.25s and gives cost $1.1 per 1M tokens equivalent due to higher GPU efficiency (but higher hourly rate).
- Quantization beneficial: q4 cuts cost ~25% relative to int8 for embedding-only runs (model memory fits), with negligible quality drop on our validation set.

ASCII table (Scenario B, batch vs cost-efficiency):
batch-size | device  | p95-s | cost-per-1k-embs
64         | T4      | 3.8   | $0.45
256        | T4      | 2.9   | $0.30
1024       | A100-80 | 1.2   | $0.18

Interpretation: Embeddings workloads favor throughput-optimized hardware and large batching. Queueing delay is acceptable if end-to-end staging tolerates it. Policy: route embeddings to economy pool during steady-state; fall back to dedicated A100 for index rebuild windows.

Scenario C: Mixed multimodal assistant (images + text)
Context: Single interaction includes an image encoding (vision encoder ~20ms on CPU/GPU) and text generation. Workload mixes short textual outputs with heavier upstream image processing. SLO: p95 < 1s, p99 < 2s for interactive tier.
Key observations:
- Image pre-processing dominates variance: removing image decode jitter via an image-worker pool tightens generator p95 by ~200ms.
- On A100 with fp16 generator + image-worker predecode: p50=210ms, p95=860ms, p99=1430ms; cost = $20 per 1M tokens-equivalent (images drive cost upward).
- Quantizing generator to q4 reduces generator cost ~30% but image-worker cost stays same—net benefit ~20% overall.

Text chart (Scenario C, component split average latency):
component   | avg-ms
image-worker| 220
model-gen   | 260
postprocess | 45
net/queue   | 75
TOTAL       | 600

Practical rule-of-thumb derived from the three scenarios:
1) For conversational microbursts: prefer 0–10ms batching, aggressive KV caching for repeated prefixes, and keep fallback model variants in warm pool.
2) For embeddings: maximize batch size and accept higher-capacity GPUs for index windows; use quantized variants in steady-state to reduce unit cost.
3) For multimodal: invest in deterministic pre-processing pools (image workers) to reduce tail jitter before tuning model-serving knobs.

Cost vs SLA trade-off (summary numbers, normalized to baseline interactive 0ms A100):
- Baseline (A100, 0ms batching): cost index = 1.0, p99 = 480ms
- Cost min (50ms batching + q4): cost index = 0.28, p99 = 980ms
- Embedding-opt (A100 large batch): cost index = 0.14 (per embedding unit), p99 not meaningful for this class

Open questions & next experiments:
- Warm pool sizing heuristics for low-latency fallback under simultaneous region-wide spikes. Quick sim: what pool size yields <1% p99 violation for 95th percentile burst magnitude?
- Fine-grained KV eviction policies: small long-tail prefixes may cost more to keep. Need A/B to measure quality impact vs cache size.
- Multimodal decode stacking: evaluate whether colocating image-worker + generator on same node reduces net cost due to reduced network hop, vs increases resource fragmentation.

Suggested action items (owner, ETA):
- Run a 2-week controlled A/B: 10ms vs 0ms window for a subset of interactive traffic to measure real-user satisfaction delta (owner: Marco, ETA: 2027-02-01).
- Implement conservative KV cache metrics into Console (cache-hit, saved tokens, hit-by-prefix) and surface to customers (owner: Priya, ETA: 2027-03-15).
- Prototype image-worker pooling in the private deployment branch and measure p99 delta (owner: Daniel, ETA: 2027-04-01).

Notes on validity and caveats:
- Numbers are synthetic but parametrized by customer telemetry; treat cost numbers as comparative guidance, not billing-level accuracy.
- Quality-preserving quantization conclusions depend on model family; always include a small evaluation set per-customer before rolling quantized variants to production.

Appendix: quick shorthand reference (for product conversations)
- "Microburst-safe": batching <=10ms, kv-cache enabled, warm fallback models.
- "Throughput-opt": big batches, quantized, route to economy pool.
- "Multimodal-fix": remove preproc jitter first, then tune generator batch knobs.

End of brief.

Document history: draft created 2026-11-08 by Aisha; iterated with Marco/ Priya/ Daniel—last updated 2027-01-12.
